name: Mere-exposure effect
statement: Seeing something repeatedly makes people like it more, with no need for the repetitions to have taught them anything about it.
meaning: The word mere is carrying the claim. Liking something more after learning it is useful is unremarkable, and the proposal is that bare repeated exposure, with no reward and no new information, is enough on its own. Zajonc's first experiment had subjects pronounce the words aloud, which he judged a possible confound, so his second used Chinese-like characters that subjects only looked at. The effect has also been reported for stimuli shown too briefly to be recognised. If that holds, the preference forms without the person knowing what they are preferring.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The monograph is "Attitudinal effects of mere exposure", issued as a Monograph Supplement, volume 9, number 2, part 2, pages 1 to 27. Its abstract names four kinds of supporting evidence, two correlational and two experimental. It opens with a newspaper story about a student who attended an Oregon State University speech class inside a black bag.

evidence: The standard procedure shows a set of unfamiliar items varying numbers of times, then asks how much the participant likes each one. Liking rises with the number of prior showings. The paradigm is easy to run, has been used for over fifty years, and appears across pictures, words, sounds and faces. A copy of Zajonc's monograph was obtained for this pass, so its own figures can be given rather than described. Experiment I counterbalanced twelve seven-letter "Turkish" words against six frequencies of 0, 1, 2, 5, 10 and 25, across 86 trials at about two seconds a card. Seventy-two subjects were run one at a time, and rated goodness rose with frequency, F = 5.64, df = 5/355, p < .001. All twelve words showed the rise, which Zajonc put at a chance likelihood of .00024. Experiment II replaced the words with Chinese-like characters taken from Hull's 1920 study and dropped the pronouncing, giving F = 4.72, p < .001, with every stimulus but one showing the effect. A further study used photographs of male Michigan State University graduates, presented to Michigan students as a test of visual memory: F = 9.96, df = 5/355, p < .001, though only 9 of the 12 faces showed the rise. Experiment IV measured skin conductance instead of liking. Fifteen subjects were run, data for one were lost to an apparatus failure, and reactivity fell as prior exposure rose, F = 4.01, df = 4/117, at the .05 level. The correlational half includes a rank correlation of .96 between 1963 farm production figures for seven vegetables and how much students said they liked them. Zajonc also reports a null he did not treat as a threat: Amster and Glasman found no exposure effect for meaningful English words, which he attributes to the words already having been seen thousands of times.

replication.headline: A meta-analysis of 268 curve estimates found an inverted U, so more exposure stops helping and starts hurting. Four later face experiments found no effect at all.
replication.detail: Montoya and colleagues pooled 268 curve estimates from 81 articles and modelled liking as a function of number of exposures rather than as a single difference. Their abstract reports a positive slope and a negative quadratic term, consistent with an inverted-U curve. It lists that shape as holding for all visual but not auditory stimuli, for exposure durations shorter than 10 seconds and longer than 1 minute, for both homogeneous and heterogeneous presentation, and for ratings taken after all stimuli had been shown. They conclude that existing models of the effect do not account for the findings. Against that sits Chow, Rhodes, Rule, Buchsbaum and Hasher, who ran four online experiments on neutral faces. They recruited 50 older and 50 younger adults for each experiment and analysed 92, 95, 96 and 96 of them after losses to missing data files and to failures to follow instructions. Repeated exposure raised liking in none of the four, and Bayes factors above 16.41 favoured the null in each. Separate analyses by age gave values for the null of 6.04, 11.32, 22.98 and 9.70 among older adults, and 11.98, 21.82, 1.76 and 10.69 among younger ones. The paper states that its hypotheses and analyses were not preregistered. So the verdict is mixed in a specific sense. The pooled curve literature says the effect is real and non-monotonic, and the best-powered set of face experiments says it is absent.

study.cite: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., Vevea, J. L., Citkowicz, M., & Lauber, E. A. (2017). A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking. Psychological Bulletin, 143(5), 459-498.

limits: No pooled effect size is printed here, and the reason is a gap rather than a judgement about the paper. The full text of Montoya and colleagues was not obtained on this pass. APA PsycNET, Ovid, ResearchGate, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Europe PMC and open-web search each returned the record and none returned the article. Everything said above about that meta-analysis is read off its abstract at PubMed, so this page makes no claim about what its tables contain. Bornstein's 1989 synthesis of the first twenty years of this literature is the other landmark review, and it is the source of the figures usually quoted for the effect. The same search reached its record at Crossref, PubMed, ProQuest, OpenAlex and APA PsycNET without reaching either the article or the APA abstract. OpenAlex holds only a French-language indexing summary of it, which lists the moderators studied and gives no figures. Its study count and its pooled correlation are therefore left out here rather than copied from secondary descriptions. Anyone citing a pooled r for mere exposure is citing Bornstein, and should read him first. The modality split matters for the uses this effect is put to: the inverted-U shape held for what people see and not for what they hear, which cuts against reasoning from this literature about repeated music or radio advertising. Two 2025 studies bear on that and postdate the last check of this page. Mavromati, Erdinch and Paterson tested Scottish-accented voices in two online studies, 238 participants hearing sentences and 88 hearing words, the second preregistered. Voices heard 8 times were liked more than unheard voices and voices heard 2 or 5 times were liked less, an inverted U in liking. Their own mixed model puts exposure group at chi-squared(3) = 14.34 with a corrected p of .064, and they read that as inadequate power rather than as support. Panagopoulos, Green and Moniz ran three sets of experiments exposing American voters to the names of little-known challengers, and report in their abstract that the results yield little support for the hypothesis that exposure raises electoral support. Their full text sits behind a Cloudflare block at SAGE and was not obtained, so nothing is quoted from it beyond the abstract deposited at Crossref. A meta-analysis also inherits whatever publication bias sits in its inputs, which for a fifty-year-old effect with an easy paradigm is a real concern.
misreadings: The effect is routinely cited as though more exposure always means more liking, which the meta-analysis specifically contradicts. It also gets used to explain advertising wearout and its opposite at the same time, which should be a warning: a claim that predicts both outcomes predicts neither. The subliminal version is the most-quoted and least-secure part of the literature. Its founding demonstration, Kunst-Wilson and Zajonc's 1980 report in Science, used two groups of 12 subjects. Octagons shown for 1 millisecond were later preferred to new ones 60 per cent of the time, chi-squared = 8.44, P < .01, while recognition ran at 48 per cent. Sixteen of the 24 preferred old to new, and 5 of the 24 recognised old stimuli above chance. De Zilva, Vu, Newell and Pearson later used continuous flash suppression to hold stimuli out of awareness, checking awareness on every trial. In their first experiment, on a convenience sample of 1,005 psychology students, liking rose with exposure for visible shapes, F(1,841) = 5.79, p = .02, d = .17, and not for suppressed ones, p = .78. The comparison that matters did not come out: awareness did not interact with exposure, F(1,544) = 1.44, p = .23, and the authors wrote that no strong conclusion about awareness could be drawn from that experiment alone. Their second experiment, on faces, gave the interaction, F(1,64) = 6.21, p = .01, across 65 participants with complete data in both conditions. So the subliminal claim rests on weaker ground than the ordinary one, which is not the same as its being refuted. Three neighbouring entries cover material that is often run together with this one. Illusory truth effect, no. 27, is repetition raising rated truth rather than rated liking. Fluency heuristic, no. 245, and familiarity heuristic, no. 256, are inference rules for choosing between two recognised options, and the fluency entry carries the processing-fluency account that is usually offered as the mechanism here.
